The Factory System. An organizational and technological framework that consolidated mass production under one roof, replacing artisanal and cottage industries with centralized, machine-driven manufacturing.

Factories centralized production because steam engines required fixed installations. Multiple machines powered from one engine were more efficient than scattered cottage operations. James Watt's improved steam engine in 1769 and Matthew Boulton's manufacturing enterprise pioneered this model. The textile industry, with its spinning and weaving, was the first to fully mechanize.

Factory production relied on division of labor. Workers performed repetitive, specialized tasks rather than mastering a complete craft. This efficiency multiplied output but deskilled labor.

Raw materials flowed into factories in unprecedented volume, and standardized products flowed out. Logistics and transportation networks—canals and railways—were reorganized accordingly.

The factory required massive capital investment in machinery. Ownership concentrated in merchant-manufacturers and early industrialists, creating a capitalist class distinct from merchants and landowners.

Workers abandoned rural life for factory towns. Crowded urban tenements, long hours from twelve to sixteen daily, dangerous conditions, and low wages characterized early factory labor.

Child labor was rampant. Children's small fingers were ideal for textile machinery, and they were cheaper than adults. Reformers did not successfully restrict child labor until the mid-eighteen-hundreds.

The factory system generated new ideologies. Socialist critique of exploitation and alienation emerged, classical economic theory justified competitive markets, and nationalist pride in productive capacity flourished.

Factory discipline introduced the time-clock, supervision hierarchies, and efficiency metrics that defined modern work. Resistance to this discipline took forms from Luddism to labor unions.
